cedVersion: Revised CED effective 2026-27 school year (first exam May 2027). Hand-curated from the July 2026 College Board PDF.
practices: The revised AP Statistics course follows the statistical problem-solving process from the ASA's GAISE II guidelines and is organized around four Statistical Practices (these REPLACE the old skill categories 'Selecting Statistical Methods', 'Data Analysis', 'Using Probability and Simulation', and 'Statistical Argumentation' — never use the old names). Practice 1, Formulate Questions (5-10% of MCQs): 1.A Determine a valid investigative question that requires a statistical investigation. Practice 2, Collect Data (20-30% of MCQs): identify and justify methods for collecting data and conducting statistical inference — 2.A Identify information to answer a question or solve a problem; 2.B Justify an appropriate method for ethically gathering and representing data; 2.C Identify appropriate statistical inference methods; 2.D Identify types of errors and relationships among components in statistical inference methods; 2.E Identify the null and alternative hypotheses. Practice 3, Analyze Data (25-35% of MCQs): construct representations of data and calculate numerical statistical outputs — 3.A Construct tabular and graphical representations of data and distributions; 3.B Calculate summary statistics, relative positions of points within a distribution, and predicted responses; 3.C Calculate and estimate expected counts, percentages, probabilities, and intervals; 3.D Calculate means, standard deviations, and parameters for probability distributions; 3.E Calculate appropriate statistical inference method results. Practice 4, Interpret Results (25-35% of MCQs): interpret results and justify conclusions and methods — 4.A Describe and compare tabular and graphical representations of data, as well as summary statistics; 4.B Justify a claim based on statistical calculations and results; 4.C Describe distributions and compare relative positions of points within a distribution; 4.D Interpret statistical calculations and results to assess meaning or a claim; 4.E Justify the use of a chosen statistical inference method by verifying conditions; 4.F Interpret results of statistical inference methods; 4.G Justify a claim based on statistical inference method results. NEW EMPHASIS: the investigative question. A statistical study collects data from a sample to answer an investigative question about a larger population. A valid investigative question has a defined purpose fixed before analysis (never changed based on results), is posed so the needed data can be collected and analyzed, and has three components: (1) it guides data collection and is phrased in terms of the variable(s) of interest; (2) it guides the analysis choice — for a hypothesis test it makes clear the parameter and the direction of the alternative (not equal, greater than, less than, association/not independent), for a confidence interval it makes clear the parameter and the goal of estimating it within a range of values; (3) it indicates the type of conclusion — the population the conclusions apply to and, for an experiment with random assignment, a cause-and-effect conclusion. Regularly ask students to write or critique investigative questions, and to connect them to the study design and the inference procedure. Both the formulating and the collecting practices are now heavily weighted, so sampling design, experimental design, and ethical data collection deserve real practice time, not just recall of vocabulary.

units.unitTitle: Exploring One-Variable Data and Collecting Data

1.2 Variables (observational units, variables, parameters, statistics)
1.3 Tabular Representation and Summary Statistics for One Categorical Variable
1.4 Graphical Representations for One Categorical Variable
1.5 Graphical Representations for One Quantitative Variable
1.6 Descriptions for One Quantitative Variable Distributions (shape, center, variability, unusual features)
1.7 Summary Statistics for One Quantitative Variable (mean, median, quartiles, IQR, range, standard deviation, percentiles; resistant vs. nonresistant measures)
1.8 Graphical Representations of Summary Statistics for One Quantitative Variable (boxplots, outliers)
1.9 Comparisons of the Distributions for One Quantitative Variable (including z-scores / standardized scores)
1.10 The Investigative Question Revisited and Data Collection (three components of an investigative question; census; experiments vs. observational studies)
1.11 Random Sampling (simple random, stratified, cluster, systematic)
1.12 Potential Problems with Sampling (sources of bias)
1.13 Experimental Design (treatments, random assignment, control, blinding, placebo, block designs, matched pairs, scope of conclusions)

examFormat.multipleChoice: 42 questions, 90 minutes, 50% of total score. Each question has FOUR answer choices (A-D). Mix of discrete questions and question sets, including one 3-question set on probability, random variables, and probability distributions and one 3-question set on regression analysis. Fully digital in Bluebook; an approved graphing calculator and Bluebook's built-in Desmos calculator are allowed; formulas and tables are provided.
examFormat.freeResponse: 4 questions, 90 minutes, 50% of total score; each question is worth 10 points (12.5% of the exam) and scored analytically. In order: Q1 Multi-Focus on Practices 1 and 2 (formulate questions and collect data); Q2 Multi-Focus on Practices 3 and 4 (analyze data and interpret results); Q3 Inference (a hypothesis test or a confidence interval, assessing Practices 2, 3, and 4); Q4 Multi-Focus on Practices 2, 3, and 4 across multiple content areas. There is NO investigative task and there are no longer 6 FRQs. Common task verbs: calculate, compare, complete, construct, describe, determine, estimate, explain, identify/classify, interpret, justify.

antiPatterns: This course follows the REVISED 2026-27 CED. Your general knowledge of AP Statistics probably reflects the old 9-unit CED, so do not rely on it for scope. REMOVED from the course — never teach, quiz, or assess these, and if a student asks, say briefly that it is no longer on the AP exam: combining random variables (sums/differences of random variables, linear transformations of random variables), the geometric distribution, chi-square goodness-of-fit tests, inference for the slope of a regression line (confidence intervals and tests for slope — the old Unit 9), analyzing departures from linearity (transformations/re-expressing data), and high-leverage or influential points in regression. Outliers in one-variable data (shown on boxplots; resistance of median/IQR) are still in scope. OLD STRUCTURE — never refer to the old unit numbers or titles (e.g., 'Unit 4 Probability', 'Unit 5 Sampling Distributions', 'Unit 8 Chi-Square', 'Unit 9 Slopes'): probability is now Unit 2, two-way tables are in Unit 2, sampling distributions are spread across Units 2-4, chi-square homogeneity/independence is in Unit 3, and regression is Unit 5 at the end of the course. OLD EXAM FORMAT — never mention an investigative task, 6 FRQs, 40 MCQs, or five answer choices. General rules: confidence interval and test statistic formulas are built from the provided formula sheet and need not be memorized; least-squares coefficients are calculated with technology; students should interpret technology output rather than doing long hand calculations. In conclusions, students 'reject' or 'fail to reject' the null hypothesis, never 'accept' or 'prove' it, and they back the decision with a comparison of the p-value to the significance level, in context.
